title: The future of some game genres?
author: AsparagusOk8818
selftext:
...So, I've been working away at a turn-based autobattler, and last night I decided I needed a bit of a break and just wanted to chuck some dice in Pathfinder 2E.

I set-up Owl Bear Rodeo, and then realized I had to reconstruct a bunch of data, which was frustrating... 

So, I thought, 'maybe ChatGPT could help manage some of the data stuff'. 

  
...Instead, ChatGPT just ran the game. And it was smooth. And... somehow, the writing was not the typical garbage you get out of ChatGPT. It was actually okay. 

I've never had a smoother experience playing a TTRPG online. It was purely superior to any VTT. 

  
...It was also better than most turn-based video games within that genre. Like... it was just better. It was the full narrative TTRPG experience, but without any of the bookkeeping, set-up, teardown, etc. It was a completely superior experience - with the caveat that this is only the case if you don't need fancy visuals.   
  
  
In the future, it's not hard to see the visual being solved, IMHO (though it is hardly a guarantee).   
  
  
...This experience has made me rethink my project. I really wonder if the better idea for coding up a game is, strangely, actually just building a rules framework and then having an LLM run that framework (at least for some types of games). 

This would not currently make sense for a lot of projects at all... but I wonder if this is the direction at least some significant slice of development is going to head in? If an LLM is being an on-the-fly director for your game, where that is viable, suddenly you don't need a bespoke AI system for your game, you don't need procedural generators... 

I was very doubtful about LLMs have a direct integration into games. After yesterday, I am much less skeptical.

comments.author: Gorebus2
comments.body: I think we've just, in the last few months, reached a point where AIs can competently run a TTRPG. I had played with it a number of times over the years and I've finally had some real success - to the point where I then proceeded to build an adventure testing harness where you can plug in a D&D adventure and have the AI run parties through it multiple times to give you stats on how the adventure plays!

replies.author: AsparagusOk8818
replies.body:
My current question is this: is it just that PF2E and D&D are so well-represented by online data sets that they are actually baked into the training data, and that's why it's so smooth? So it's not really replicable to other systems? 

Or could you try to build an LLM-friendly system and it would work? 

I tried running Outgunned, and it went horribly. Complete disaster. But I suspect that's because Outgunned is just contained in a PDF, which isn't easily readable for the machine. 

I might try building a system that's built using markdown files and just see how that goes...
